text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:

- Debate about solidarity tax continues in government. Finance Minister Theo Waigel does not agree with FDP demands to create separate law for cutting the tax in the event that tax reform bill fails to win legislative approval. FDP insists that solidarity tax must be cut.

- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel guarantees Russia that it will be included. One week after NATO announces enlargement plans, Kinkel tells Russian foreign minister that Russia will be included in European security order.

- Statistics office says 85 percent of German schoolchildren learn foreign langauge. Two-thirds learn English, about 18 percent learn French, 11 percent learn Latin. Interest in Russian falls sharply by 40 percent.
- Fronts harden in Bonn coalition over tax cuts. FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt calls it typical summer theatre while Finance Minster Theo Waigel sticks to firm position.
- German federal court rules that banks cannot charge customers for tax-exempt forms for interest income.

- Frankfurt bourse police (BAWe) pursuing more insider trading violations. In first half of 1997 agency uncovers 15 cases that it passes along to state prosecutors office, compared to 17 in all of 1996. But head of agency says that number of insider violations has not suddenly begun to rise, rather agency has become more efficient in tracking violations.
- Trial of former construction magnate Juergen Schneider to continue on Wednesday after court session cancelled on Tuesday due to illness of one judge.

- Germany makes great progress in environmental protection. Cleanliness of air, water and ground in Germany has improved dramatically in recent years, according to report by Federal Environmental Office (UBA).
